title: Types of Discontinuity: Infinite
notes: **Definition.** f has an infinite discontinuity at a when f(x) grows without bound as x → a from at least one side, so the graph has a vertical asymptote x = a.
**Worked example.** For f(x) = 1/(x − 2), lim(x→2⁻) = −∞ and lim(x→2⁺) = +∞; the two sides disagree in sign and neither is finite.
**Finding asymptotes.** In a rational function, cancel common factors first; the remaining zeros of the denominator give the vertical asymptotes, while cancelled zeros give holes.
**One-sided signs.** Determine the sign of the unbounded limit by testing a nearby value on each side rather than by assuming symmetry.
**Contrast.** A removable hole has a finite two-sided limit; an infinite discontinuity has no finite limit, so it cannot be repaired by redefining f(a).
**Exam caution.** Writing lim = ∞ is a description of unbounded growth, not a real number; a question asking whether the limit exists expects 'no finite limit'.
summary: An infinite discontinuity occurs at a vertical asymptote where at least one one-sided limit is unbounded; no finite limit exists at that point.
